target: 오늘 밤에 시험 공부를 할 거예요.
english: I'll study for the exam tonight.
tip: 시험 공부 (siheom gongbu) = studying FOR an exam — nouns stack directly in Korean.

english: I'll take an exam next week.
tip: Korean 'sees' exams: 시험을 봐요 (siheomeul bwayo = take a test).

english: I'll study at the library for three hours.
tip: 시 (si) vs 시간 (sigan): 세 시 (se si) = 3 o'clock, but 세 시간 (se sigan) = 3 hours. Adding 간 (gan) turns clock time into a duration.

english: I'll go to bed at eleven.
tip: 잘 거예요 (jal geoyeyo) here is 자다 (jada = sleep), not 잘 (jal = well) – they look identical. 'Will sleep' vs 'well': context decides.
언제 (eonje = when) never takes 에: 언제 올 거예요? = when will you come?
누구 + 가 contracts: 누가 (nuga = who, as the subject).
씨 (ssi) after a name = polite 'Mr/Ms': 수진 씨 (Sujin ssi). Never attach it to your own name, and never use it alone.

english: We'll meet in front of the cafe.
tip: Meeting spots take 에서: 앞에서 만날 거예요 (apeseo mannal geoyeyo = we'll meet in front).
Time 'catches' in Korean: 걸리다 (geollida = to take time, literally 'to hang, catch'). 얼마나 걸릴 거예요? (eolmana geollil geoyeyo) = how long will it take?
분 (bun = minutes) takes Sino numbers: 삼십 분 (samsip bun = 30 minutes).
다 잘 될 거예요 (da jal doel geoyeyo) — Korea's favorite reassurance: 'it'll all work out.'
내일 봐요 (naeil bwayo = see you tomorrow) — present form, future meaning.
배고파요 (baegopayo = I'm hungry) — no pronoun needed; Korean drops "I".
안 (an = not) goes right before the verb, no helper needed: 안 먹었어요 (an meogeosseoyo) = didn't eat. Korean has no "do" for negatives.
점심 먹었어요? (jeomsim meogeosseoyo) doubles as a friendly greeting, like "how's it going?"
목말라요 (mongmallayo = I'm thirsty) — 목 (throat) + 마르다 (to be dry).
Questions don't rearrange anything – 저녁 먹었어요? (jeonyeok meogeosseoyo) is the exact statement with rising tone. No "did you" flip.

english: This restaurant is famous for bulgogi.
tip: Two subjects, no problem: 이 식당은 (i sikdang-eun) sets the topic, 불고기가 (bulgogi-ga) is the subject – "as for this place, the bulgogi is famous."
뭐가 맛있어요? (mwoga masisseoyo = what's tasty?) — ask staff; they love recommending.

english: This place is famous for cold noodles.
tip: 집 (jip = house) also means a go-to eatery: 냉면 집 = a naengmyeon place.
을/를 (eul/reul) tags the object: 한국 음식을 (hanguk eumsigeul = Korean food). Once tagged it can move around the sentence – the verb just stays last.
있어요 (isseoyo) covers both "there is" and "have": 자리 있어요? (jari isseoyo) is literally "does a seat exist?" – no separate verb for "have."

english: Two servings of pork belly, please.
tip: 인분 (inbun = serving) takes Sino numbers: 2인분 reads 이인분 (i-inbun), never native 두 (du). Each counter picks its own number system.
Ordering with 하나 (hana = one) after the dish name is the everyday pattern.
셀프 (selpeu = self-serve) — at many Korean restaurants you fetch water yourself.
도 (do = also) replaces 은/는/이/가: 밥도 = rice too.
저기요 (jeogiyo = excuse me) is the polite way to call restaurant staff.
마리 (mari) counts animals — and whole chickens on menus: 한 마리 (han mari).
Korean flips "a bottle of soju": the drink comes first, then number + counter – 소주 한 병 (soju han byeong = soju one bottle).
나오다 (naoda = to come out) is how Koreans say food arrives: 나왔어요.
